deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the R.Ellipsoid bundle, which belongs to Riemann's work on the motion of a homogeneous, self-gravitating liquid ellipsoid. That work was published as 'Ein Beitrag zu den Untersuchungen über die Bewegung eines gleichartigen flüssigen Ellipsoides' (Abh. Göttingen 9, 1861). The page is a fragment: a single continued sentence, a sketch and a row of symbols. No derivation is carried out here.

(1) The sentence. It begins '...bezeichnet;', so H was defined on the preceding (lost or other) sheet.
- My inference, not on the page: H is almost certainly the gravitational quantity of the ellipsoid with semi-axes a, b, c at fixed volume (abc = const). That is H = ∫_0^∞ ds / sqrt((a^2+s)(b^2+s)(c^2+s)), up to a constant factor. The self-potential energy is W = -(3/10) G M^2 H, which gives -3GM^2/(5R) for the sphere.
- The text says, in modern terms:
  - (i) H → 0 when one axis → 0. Because abc is fixed, at least one other axis must then → ∞ ('und folglich wenigstens eine der andern unendlich wird').
  - (ii) When the axes b (and probably c) grow without bound, H only decreases ('nimmt ... nur ab').
- Purpose: to establish the boundary behaviour of an energy-type function on the set of ellipsoids of given volume. This is the standard existence argument: the energy function of the axes must attain an extremum in the interior, which gives an equilibrium or stable figure. Riemann uses this kind of argument for the existence and stability of equilibrium figures (§§ on stability in the 1861 paper).
- Supporting estimate (mine): take a → 0 with b → ∞ and c fixed. Then H ≤ ∫_0^∞ ds / (sqrt(s) sqrt(b^2+s) sqrt(c^2+s)), which is of order (2/b) log(b/c) → 0. If instead b = c → ∞ (a flat disc), H ~ π/b → 0. So claim (i) is correct.

(2) The sketch. An ellipse with axes labelled b (horizontal) and c (vertical) is inscribed in a circle, with several diameters drawn. This is the b-c principal section of the ellipsoid compared with a circumscribed circle. The diameters suggest a direction (an angle) in that plane, as when one decomposes a rotation or an internal vortex vector in the b-c plane.

(3) The symbol row: b q_1, c r_1, r b, q c, sqrt(q_1^2 + r_1^2).
- These are products of axis lengths with Riemann's rotation/vortex components. In the 1861 paper, p, q, r and p_1, q_1, r_1 (or primed versions) denote the angular-velocity and internal-motion components.
- So these are velocity amplitudes in the b-c section, e.g. vectors (b q_1, c r_1) or (r b, q c). The modulus sqrt(q_1^2 + r_1^2) is the magnitude of the vortex component lying in that plane.
- Nothing further is computed on this page.

The next page (τ'^2/(ε π ρ^4) as a function of an angle ψ, with logarithmic numerics) evaluates an equilibrium or stability condition numerically for a particular figure. That is consistent with the present page being part of Riemann's stability discussion.
errors: No computational errors are visible; the page contains only qualitative statements.
Claim (i) is correct as stated: with abc fixed, flattening one axis to zero forces another to infinity, and the energy integral H tends to 0.

Claim (ii) is too terse to check: 'wenn b ... unendlich wächst nur ab' presumably asserts monotone decrease along such a path. That holds for the natural paths (e.g. b = c increasing with a = V/b^2), but not along arbitrary paths, since H is maximal at the sphere. Riemann's intended path is not stated on this sheet.

results.what: Boundary behaviour of the ellipsoid self-energy integral H = ∫ ds/Δ at fixed volume: H → 0 when one axis → 0 (so another → ∞), and H decreases as axes grow unboundedly. This is used to secure an interior extremum, i.e. existence of an equilibrium figure.
results.modern_name: Gravitational self-energy of a homogeneous ellipsoid; variational existence argument for ellipsoidal equilibrium figures
results.usually_credited_to: Energy integral: Dirichlet/Dedekind/Jacobi tradition (19th c.); variational existence and stability arguments: Riemann 1861, later Poincaré 1885 and Lyapunov

results.what: Sketch of the b-c principal section inscribed in a circle, together with the combinations b q_1, c r_1, r b, q c, sqrt(q_1^2+r_1^2) for rotation/vortex components in that plane
results.modern_name: Riemann ellipsoids (rotation plus uniform internal vorticity), decomposition of the vorticity vector
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1861 (Riemann ellipsoids, building on Dirichlet 1857/1860 and Dedekind)

deep.surprise_reason: This is preparatory material for Riemann's published 1861 memoir on liquid ellipsoids. The energy-boundary argument and the rotation/vortex variables are known parts of that work. The page adds no new result.

checkable.asserts: For the sphere, H = 2/R, so W = -(3/10) G M^2 H = -3GM^2/(5R).
In the flat-disc limit (a → 0, b = c → ∞), H ~ π/b → 0.
The disc-limit integral equals π/b exactly (b > 0).

transcription_corrections: '[-wenigstens-]': in the image the word before 'eine der andern' is struck through and stands in the line (read: 'folglich ~~wenigstens~~ eine der andern unendlich wird'). Its sense is still 'at least one'.

'wenn b in b unendlich wächst' is doubtful. The image reads more like 'wenn b und c unendlich wächst' or 'wenn b' u. b unendlich wächst'. The second symbol should be checked; 'b und c' fits the sense best.
The figure labels are 'c' (vertical semi-axis) and 'b' (horizontal semi-axis) of an ellipse inscribed in a circle. Several diameters or chords are drawn, one of them oblique.
The bottom row reads 'bq_1, cr_1, r,b, q,c, sqrt(q_1^2+r_1^2)'. The commas after r and q are probably subscript-like marks, i.e. 'r_1 b' or 'r, b' (unclear).
